desc:
Given two strings s and t, return the length of the longest string that appears in both of them as a contiguous block of characters (a substring, not merely a subsequence).

If the strings have no character in common, or one of them is empty, the answer is 0.

s = "xabcdy", t = "zzabcdq"  ->  4   ("abcd")
s = "abab",   t = "baba"     ->  3   ("aba" or "bab")
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Try every pair of starting positions and extend while the characters keep matching. That works, but it repeats a lot of comparisons. How could you reuse the work of a previous pair?
Let L(i, j) be the length of the longest common block that ends exactly at position i of s and position j of t. If the two characters differ, L(i, j) = 0; otherwise L(i, j) = L(i-1, j-1) + 1.
The answer is the maximum value of L(i, j) over all cells, not the last cell. Each row only needs the row above it, so two arrays of length t.length + 1 are enough.
editorial: Define L[i][j] as the length of the longest common substring that ends at s[i-1] and t[j-1]. A common block that ends at these two positions must either be empty (the characters differ) or be one character longer than the block ending at the previous pair of positions, so L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1] + 1 when the characters match and 0 otherwise.

Unlike the subsequence version, a mismatch resets the run to zero instead of carrying the best value forward, because the block must stay contiguous. The answer is the largest value seen anywhere in the table. Keeping only the previous row gives O(t.length) memory. Comparing every pair of start positions and extending is O(m · n · min(m, n)) in the worst case, far too slow at the upper limits.
